Drought
DROWT
noun
From the Saxon drugothe, dryness, from drigan, to dry; hence a want of rain, the parching of the ground — and in Scripture, by a bold figure, the parching of a man’s own soul under the hand of God.

Biblical Definition

Drought is the withholding of rain, and it is one of the plainest instruments of covenant discipline, because in Canaan there were no great rivers to fall back upon: Israel drank from heaven or not at all. Moses warned that disobedience would shut up the heaven that there be no rain (Deu 11:17); Elijah shut it by prayer for three years and a half in Ahab’s reign (1Ki 17:1); Haggai reports the LORD saying flatly, “I called for a drought upon the land” (Hag 1:11), and the drought lay upon the corn, the new wine, the oil, and upon the labour of men’s hands. Jacob knew drought as the herdsman’s ordinary hardship, consumed by heat in the day and frost by night (Gen 31:40). But the sharpest use of the word is inward. David, silent about his sin, describes the wasting of a conscience under conviction: “For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me: my moisture is turned into the drought of summer” (Psa 32:4). An unconfessed sin dries a man out. And against that stands Jeremiah’s picture of the man whose trust is in the LORD: a tree planted by the waters, whose leaf is green, which “shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit” (Jer 17:8). Drought judges the shallow-rooted and proves the deep-rooted; the same dry season declares both.

Webster 1828 Definition

Dryness; want of rain; and figuratively the parching of the soul under unconfessed sin — a season that exposes shallow roots and proves deep ones.

DROUGHT, dryness; want of rain or of water; thirst; want of drink.

From the Saxon drugothe, dryness, from drigan, to dry.

Applied to the parched state of the ground and to the wasting of the body or spirit for want of moisture.

Hebrew choreb, parching heat, and tsimmaon, a thirsty ground (Deu 8:15).

Psa 32:4 uses it of the soul: “my moisture is turned into the drought of summer.”

Key Scripture

Psa 32:4 — "For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me: my moisture is turned into the drought of summer. Selah."

Jer 17:8 — "For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river, and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit."

Hag 1:11 — "And I called for a drought upon the land, and upon the mountains, and upon the corn, and upon the new wine, and upon the oil, and upon that which the ground bringeth forth, and upon men, and upon cattle, and upon all the labour of the hands."

Gen 31:40 — "Thus I was; in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep departed from mine eyes."

Modern Corruption

The inward drought is the one modern readers skip. Dryness of soul is diagnosed as a mood or a season to be waited out, when David traces it to a specific sin he would not name.

expand to see more

Psalm 32 is precise, and the precision is what gets lost. David does not say he passed through a dry stretch; he says God’s hand was heavy upon him day and night, that his bones waxed old through his roaring all the day long, and that his moisture was turned into the drought of summer — and he tells us exactly why: “When I kept silence.” The cause was concealed sin, and the cure was not the passage of time but confession: “I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin.” The counsel commonly given to a dried-out believer never gets near this. He is told his dryness is a phase, that everyone has them, that he should rest and be patient with himself. Sometimes that is true — there is a genuine dryness under affliction, and the saints have written of it honestly. But the first question David’s psalm puts is the one seldom asked: is there something you are keeping silence about? To skip that question is to leave a man roaring all the day long with the remedy in his hand and no one to tell him to open it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God appoints the dry season on purpose and provides against it beforehand. Jeremiah’s contrast is between the heath in the desert, which shall not see when good cometh, and the tree planted by the waters, which does not even notice the year of drought because its roots went for the river long before the rain stopped. Roots are grown in ordinary weather. The believer who reads, prays, sits under faithful preaching, and keeps short accounts with God in a green year is quietly sending roots toward the river; the one who lives on surface rain finds out what he was living on the first summer it fails. And when the drought is inward and does come, the LORD does not leave His people to it: “I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground” (Isa 44:3). He who called for the drought is the same who ends it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Want of rain upon the ground, and want of moisture in the soul; a season appointed to expose what a man’s roots have been reaching for.

expand to see more

Drought — Saxon drugothe, dryness, from drigan, to dry.

Hebrew choreb (parching heat) and tsimmaon (a thirsty land, Deu 8:15).

Deu 11:17 — disobedience shuts up the heaven that there be no rain.

Hag 1:11 — “I called for a drought upon the land”: the LORD names Himself the cause.

Psa 32:4 turns the word inward: conviction of unconfessed sin dries a man out.

Usage

"In Canaan there were no great rivers — Israel drank from heaven or not at all."

"David’s drought of summer had a cause he names: when I kept silence."

"Roots are grown in green years; the dry year only shows where they already went."
